column3: Eberwin of Steinfeld reports a group with Cathar-like beliefs at Cologne, the first confirmed report of identifiable Catharism.
A council at Saint-Félix-Lauragais gathers Cathar leaders from the Languedoc, northern France and Lombardy with the Bogomil papa Nicetas.
Many towns of Provence and its vicinity are almost wholly Cathar, and the Pope turns to crusade after the legate Castelnau is murdered in 1208.
The Albigensian Crusade begins with the massacre at Béziers, and runs for twenty years of war in the Languedoc.
The Treaty of Paris ends the official war, but Catholic forces keep pursuing Cathars.
The Inquisition is established and works at Toulouse, Albi, Carcassonne and other towns through the 13th century and much of the 14th.
Montségur falls and over 200 Cathar Perfects are burned, while the survivors scatter as fugitives.
Peire Autier, leader of a revival in the Pyrenean foothills, is executed at Toulouse.
Guillaume Bélibaste, the last known Cathar Perfect in the Languedoc, is executed.
The Inquisition claims to have eradicated the Cathars; records after 1330 hold very few proceedings against them.
